notes: Rumor II (Aug 1969 to Mar 1970) is a DC single-party cabinet with outside support from PSI, PSU and PRI; the template coalition slot 2 holds La Malfa's PRI as the centre-left's liberal partner. The PLI takes slot 16 (free-market liberals, popularity matching its 5.8 percent) instead of MD's Radical Party, which gets no slot; MD's slot-2 Federazione dei Liberali is a 1994 PLI heir. Social-democratic PSU sits in slot 3, De Martino's PSI as non-aligned socialists in 18 (PSIUP left out). The MSI takes slot 20 (MD's AN, with popularity), the revolutionary Ordine Nuovo split slot 21. Slots 8, 9 and 12 are catchy student circles.

0.name: Fronte Nazionale
0.text:
The National Front was founded in 1968 by Prince Junio Valerio Borghese, the 'Black Prince' who commanded the Decima MAS naval commandos for Mussolini's Social Republic and briefly presided over the MSI. It recruits retired officers, former paratroopers, monarchists and neo-fascist street fighters, and cultivates contacts in the armed forces, the Carabinieri and the secret services.

After the strikes of the Hot Autumn and the Piazza Fontana bombing of December 1969, Borghese claims that only a strong presidential order can save Italy from communism. He wants to outlaw the PCI, curb the unions and keep Italy firmly in NATO, counting on American sympathy. Its leverage lies in its links with officers and policemen and in the fears of a frightened bourgeoisie.

1.name: Democrazia Cristiana
1.text:
Christian Democracy has been Italy's ruling party since 1946 and the bulwark of the West against the largest communist party in the Western world, winning 39.1 percent in 1968. Prime Minister Mariano Rumor, a leader of the dominant Dorotei faction, heads a single-party cabinet that relies on Socialist, Social Democratic and Republican support, while Arnaldo Forlani became party secretary in November 1969.

The party stands for NATO, European integration, Catholic social teaching and the centre-left formula of planned reform, now strained by the Hot Autumn and the Piazza Fontana massacre. It is a federation of currents around Moro, Fanfani, Andreotti and Donat-Cattin. Its power rests on the Church, Catholic Action, the farmers' and workers' associations and a vast system of state patronage.

2.name: Partito Repubblicano Italiano
2.text:
The Italian Republican Party, heir to Giuseppe Mazzini and founded in 1895, is small but influential, winning 2 percent in 1968. Its secretary Ugo La Malfa, a former budget minister who championed economic planning, supports Rumor's government from outside and acts as the stern conscience of the centre-left alliance.

The Republicans stand for a secular state, rigorous public finances, an incomes policy to tame inflation, modern economic planning and the defence of the lira, and they are among the most convinced Atlanticists and Europeanists in Italy. Their voters are professionals, managers and the secular middle class of Romagna and the big cities. Their leverage lies in La Malfa's authority and their pivotal role in every centre-left majority.

3.name: Partito Socialista Unitario
3.text:
The Unitary Socialist Party is the social-democratic wing that walked out of the reunited Socialist party in July 1969, accusing its partners of drifting towards the Communists. Heir to Giuseppe Saragat's 1947 breakaway from the PSI, it is led by secretary Mauro Ferri and Mario Tanassi, while Saragat himself sits in the Quirinale as President of the Republic.

It stands for Western social democracy on the Scandinavian and German model, unswerving loyalty to NATO and the United States, firm anti-communism and gradual reform within the centre-left coalition. Its voters are civil servants, white-collar employees and northern artisans, and it leans on the UIL trade union. Its leverage lies in its indispensable seats and in Saragat's power at the top of the state.

4.name: Partito Comunista Italiano
4.text:
The Italian Communist Party is the largest communist party in the West, winning 26.9 percent in 1968 and running the city halls of the red belt of Emilia, Tuscany and Umbria. Its general secretary Luigi Longo, a veteran of the Spanish Civil War and the Resistance, is grooming Enrico Berlinguer, elected deputy secretary in 1969, as his successor.

Faithful to Togliatti's Italian road to socialism, the PCI seeks power through democracy and mass struggle, defends the constitution and condemned the invasion of Czechoslovakia, yet it remains tied to Moscow by history, money and ideology. It calls for Italy's exit from NATO, economic planning and structural reforms. Its leverage lies in the CGIL unions, the cooperatives and a party of some 1.5 million members.

5.name: Lotta Continua
5.text:
Continuous Struggle was born in Turin in the autumn of 1969, when student militants led by Adriano Sofri joined the assemblies of workers striking at Fiat Mirafiori during the Hot Autumn. Its newspaper Lotta Continua spreads the gospel of workers' autonomy from Turin to Milan, Pisa and Rome, in fierce rivalry with Potere Operaio.

It rejects the PCI and the unions as tamers of the class struggle, demands equal wage rises for all and an end to piecework and murderous line speeds, and preaches direct action in factories, schools and neighbourhoods. It denounces the arrest of anarchists for the Piazza Fontana massacre and the death of Giuseppe Pinelli in police custody as a state frame-up. Its leverage lies in young workers, students and southern migrants in the northern factories.

6.name: Nazimaoisti
6.text:
The Nazi-Maoists, as the press calls them, are a fringe of young neo-fascists who despise the MSI's Atlanticism and preach a revolutionary alliance with the far left against the bourgeois order. Their theorist is the Padua publisher Franco Freda, whose 1969 tract 'The Disintegration of the System' calls for an organic, anti-capitalist state, while veterans of Jean Thiriart's pan-European Giovane Europa add their anti-American creed.

They hail Mao's China, North Vietnam and the Palestinian fedayeen as fellow fighters against American imperialism and Zionism, reject both liberal democracy and consumer society, and dream of a Europe freed from Washington's tutelage. Small and conspiratorial, they slip into leftist circles and campuses. Their leverage lies in provocation, secrecy and contacts with Arab revolutionaries.

7.name: I carristi
7.text:
The Tankmen is the nickname for the Communists who cheered the Soviet tanks in Budapest in 1956 and in Prague in 1968, against their party's official dissent. They are strongest among old partisans and cadres in Emilia and Tuscany and in the PCI's commercial and organisational apparatus, and they revere Pietro Secchia, Togliatti's hardline deputy, ousted in the mid-1950s but still a senator.

They see the Soviet Union as the fatherland of socialism and Togliatti's Italian road as a slide into social democracy. Their ideal is a people's democracy on the Eastern model, out of NATO and allied to the Warsaw Pact. Their leverage lies in Moscow's funds flowing through import-export firms, in the party's old clandestine apparatus and in the loyalty of its veterans.

8.name: Circolo Bazargan
8.text:
The Bazargan Circle gathers devout Iranian students in Rome, Perugia and Florence who admire Mehdi Bazargan, the engineer and Muslim reformer whose banned Freedom Movement of Iran has seen its leaders jailed by the Shah, and who pass around the lectures of Ali Shariati in Tehran. They keep apart from the Marxist-led Iranian student confederation active in Italian universities.

They seek a constitutional Iran free of the Shah's dictatorship and of American tutelage, where an Islam renewed by science and reason inspires social justice and national independence, and they reject both clerical rule and communism. Their influence in Italy is negligible, but these future engineers and doctors are preparing to carry their ideas back home.

9.name: Cerchia di Qom
9.text:
The Qom Circle is a small band of Iranian theology students and merchants in Rome and Milan loyal to Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, the Shah's fiercest clerical foe, exiled since 1964 and teaching in Najaf. They distribute his letters and taped sermons, collect religious dues for his representatives and keep a wary eye on the informers of the Iranian embassy.

They call for the Shah's overthrow and an Islamic order guided by the Shia jurists, denounce the White Revolution, the monarchy's ties with America and its tacit alliance with Israel, and hold communism to be as godless as the West. Their leverage in Italy is non-existent, but they are a link in the chain binding the exiled Ayatollah to the seminaries of Qom.

10.name: Centro Islamico Culturale d'Italia
10.text:
The Islamic Cultural Centre of Italy was founded in Rome in 1966 by the ambassadors of Muslim states, to serve a tiny community of diplomats, students and migrants from Libya, Somalia, Egypt and the Middle East. Its great ambition is to build the first mosque in the capital of Catholicism, an idea that still meets resistance in the city and the Church.

It represents official, conservative Sunni Islam, with Saudi Arabia, the Muslim World League and King Faisal's diplomacy as its patrons. It shuns politics, seeks recognition from the Italian state and cultivates dialogue with the Vatican in the spirit of the Second Vatican Council. Its leverage lies in oil-rich patrons and diplomatic prestige rather than in members.

11.name: Hizb ut-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir was founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by the Islamic judge Taqiuddin al-Nabhani and is outlawed throughout the Arab world for trying to recruit army officers for coups, most recently in Jordan. In Italy its message circulates among Jordanian, Palestinian and Syrian students at the universities of Perugia, Rome, Padua and Bologna, far from the reach of their home countries' police.

The party rejects nationalism, democracy and every existing Muslim regime, calling for a single caliphate to unite the Muslim world under the sharia and to confront American and Soviet power alike. It prefers secret study circles and leaflets to violence. Its leverage in Italy is negligible, but it trains cadres who will return to the Middle East.

12.name: Fratellanza di Perugia
12.text:
The Perugia Brotherhood is a circle of devout Arab students, many from Syria, Jordan and Egypt, at the University for Foreigners in Perugia and other Italian campuses, inspired by Muslim Brotherhood exiles and by Said Ramadan's Islamic Centre in Geneva. They run prayer rooms and study groups and read the works of Hasan al-Banna and of Sayyid Qutb, hanged by Nasser in 1966.

They seek a gradual Islamic renewal of society and state under the sharia, rejecting Nasser's Arab socialism, Baathism and communism and condemning Western support for Israel. Pious, disciplined and well educated, they shun violence in Italy and aim to build Muslim institutions in Europe. Their leverage lies in their organisation, Gulf patrons and the future careers of their members.

13.name: Ente Nazionale Idrocarburi
13.text:
The National Hydrocarbons Agency is the state energy giant that Enrico Mattei built after 1953 into a power in its own right, defying the Anglo-American oil majors with deals with Iran, Algeria's rebels and the Soviet Union before his death in a mysterious plane crash in 1962. Under its president Eugenio Cefis it is expanding into chemicals and quietly buying into Montedison.

ENI pursues national energy independence, a Mediterranean policy friendly to the Arab world and business with Moscow, whatever NATO may think. Its technocrats see themselves as the real state, above the squabbling parties. Their leverage lies in vast resources, secret funds for friendly politicians, the newspaper Il Giorno and networks in the ministries and the intelligence services.

14.name: Confederazione Nazionale Coltivatori Diretti
14.text:
The National Confederation of Direct Cultivators is the great Catholic union of small farmers, built since 1944 by Paolo Bonomi into one of the pillars of Christian Democratic power. Organising well over a million farming families, it controls the Federconsorzi agricultural consortia, the farmers' health insurance funds and a bloc of loyal deputies in parliament.

It defends peasant smallholdings, guaranteed prices and generous EEC farm subsidies, preaches Catholic family values and fights the communist peasant leagues in the countryside. Wary of both big capital and the left, it cares more for the village than for world affairs. Its leverage lies in the rural vote of the Po valley, the Veneto and the South and in the patronage of the agricultural bureaucracy.

15.name: Confederazione Generale dell'Industria Italiana
15.text:
The General Confederation of Italian Industry speaks for the owners of Italy's factories, from Gianni Agnelli's Fiat empire and the Pirelli group to thousands of family firms in Lombardy and Piedmont. Its president, the Genoese industrialist Angelo Costa, has just watched the Hot Autumn force through the metalworkers' contract of December 1969, with large wage rises and a shorter working week.

Confindustria defends private enterprise, managerial authority and wage discipline, fears the planned Workers' Statute and the advance of the unions, and resents the state giants of IRI and ENI. It finances the DC, the Liberals and the Social Democrats. Its leverage lies in investment decisions, the threat of capital flight to Switzerland and its owners' grip on the great newspapers.

16.name: Partito Liberale Italiano
16.text:
The Italian Liberal Party, heir to the liberal ruling class of Cavour and Giolitti, has been led since 1954 by secretary Giovanni Malagodi, a former banker who turned it into the party of free enterprise. It fought the centre-left and the nationalisation of electricity and won 5.8 percent in 1968 as the main secular opposition on the right.

The Liberals defend the market economy, private property, balanced budgets and the rule of law, warn that the new regions will hand power to the Communists, and are firmly Atlanticist and European. Yet their deputy Antonio Baslini co-sponsors the divorce bill. Their base is the northern bourgeoisie, the professions and business circles, and their leverage lies in money and the economic establishment.

17.name: Italia Nostra
17.text:
Italia Nostra was founded in Rome in 1955 by a group of intellectuals to save the country's historic towns, monuments and landscapes from destruction and speculation. Its president is the novelist Giorgio Bassani, author of The Garden of the Finzi-Continis, and the journalist Antonio Cederna is its sharpest pen against the builders who are devouring coastlines and city outskirts.

It campaigns to protect the Appian Way, Venice after the flood of 1966, the historic centres and the national parks, and demands strict town planning against the speculative building boom and the pollution of the economic miracle. Above parties and largely bourgeois, it shapes opinion more than votes. Its leverage lies in prestige, the press and the support of scholars and magistrates.

18.name: Partito Socialista Italiano
18.text:
The Italian Socialist Party, founded in 1892, stands alone again since its social democrats walked out in July 1969, ending the short-lived reunification of 1966. Its secretary Francesco De Martino and the party president Pietro Nenni, the grand old man who led it into the centre-left, back Rumor's government from outside while seeking new allies on the left.

The PSI wants 'more advanced equilibria' that would draw the Communists into dialogue, the long-delayed regions, a Workers' Statute, divorce and school reform, and an active policy of détente including recognition of the People's Republic of China. Its base lies among northern workers, the socialist wing of the CGIL, intellectuals and southern clienteles. Its leverage lies in its role as the hinge of every majority.

19.name: Il Manifesto
19.text:
Il Manifesto is the group of Communist dissidents around the monthly review of the same name, launched in June 1969 by Rossana Rossanda, Luigi Pintor, Aldo Natoli, Lucio Magri and Luciana Castellina. After its editorial 'Prague is alone' attacked the Soviet normalisation of Czechoslovakia, the PCI Central Committee expelled its founders in November 1969 for factionalism.

The group calls for a communism built from below on workers' councils and the struggles of the Hot Autumn, criticises Soviet bureaucracy and the PCI's parliamentary moderation, and looks with sympathy on the anti-bureaucratic message of the Chinese Cultural Revolution. Independent of Moscow and Washington alike, it bridges the old party and the new left. Its leverage lies in its brilliant intellectuals and growing readership.

20.name: Movimento Sociale Italiano
20.text:
The Italian Social Movement was founded in 1946 by veterans of Mussolini's Social Republic and is the main neo-fascist force in parliament, winning 4.5 percent in 1968. In June 1969 Giorgio Almirante, a former official of the Salò regime and a gifted orator, became secretary, and in November he brought Pino Rauti and many Ordine Nuovo hardliners back into the fold.

The MSI calls for a strong presidential state, corporatist representation of producers, law and order against strikes and the student revolt, and the outlawing of communism, while accepting NATO as a shield against Moscow. It speaks to the frightened middle classes, southern conservatives and nationalist youth. Its leverage lies in its militants, its youth front and its sympathisers in the police and the armed forces.

21.name: Movimento Politico Ordine Nuovo
21.text:
The New Order Political Movement was formed in December 1969 by Clemente Graziani and the militants of Pino Rauti's Ordine Nuovo study centre who refused to follow Rauti back into the MSI. Founded in 1956 on the ideas of Julius Evola, Ordine Nuovo has adopted the SS motto 'Our honour is called loyalty' and openly admires the Greek colonels.

It rejects democracy, parties, capitalism and communism alike and wants a hierarchical, spiritual and warrior state inspired by Evola's traditionalism. Its cells, strongest in Rome and the Veneto, train for the coming confrontation with the left and attract the attention of the police. Its leverage lies in fanatical cadres, hidden weapons and murky contacts in the security services.

22.name: Forze Armate Italiane
22.text:
The Italian Armed Forces, a conscript army, navy and air force of some 400,000 men guarding NATO's southern flank and the north-eastern frontier, include the Carabinieri as a military police force present in every town. They still live with the scandal over the military intelligence's secret files and the Solo Plan of 1964, when General Giovanni De Lorenzo prepared lists for mass arrests of the left.

The officer corps is conservative, monarchist in sentiment and fiercely anti-communist, and some generals see the Hot Autumn and the street violence as signs of a coming collapse. Loyal to NATO, they would act as guardians of order if the state faltered. Their leverage lies in their monopoly of force, the intelligence service SID and their American allies.

23.name: Casa Savoia
23.text:
The House of Savoy reigned over Italy from unification until the referendum of June 1946 abolished the monarchy. King Umberto II, the 'May King', lives in exile at Cascais in Portugal, barred with his male heirs from Italian soil by the constitution, while his son Vittorio Emanuele, Prince of Naples, lives in Geneva.

Monarchism survives in the South, among army veterans and the old aristocracy, in the Italian Monarchist Union and in Alfredo Covelli's Italian Democratic Party of Monarchist Unity, which won 1.3 percent in 1968. Royalists dream of a crowned, Catholic and anti-communist Italy above the parties. Their leverage lies in nostalgia, in Naples and in the loyalty of part of the officer corps.
